theme: Job curses the day; Eliphaz responds, suffering as punishment
readingInstruction: Read Job 3:1-4:21. Chapter 3 is Job’s lament, and chapter 4 is the first speech of his friend Eliphaz. Read them as a conversation between a man in pain and a man with a theory.
settingTheScene: After seven days of silence, Job finally speaks. What comes out is not a prayer to God and not a complaint about the friends. It is a wish to have never been born. The friends who sat silently beside him now begin to talk, and the rest of the book is a series of speeches. Most of Job is written in Hebrew poetry, and it is some of the most difficult poetry in the Bible. The speakers are not always right. The narrator does not tell you in each chapter who is right, so you must read with attention.
observation: Job begins, “Let the day perish on which I was born” (3:3). He wishes the day had been darkness.
He asks why he was not stillborn, and why light is given to those in misery (3:11-20).
He says that death would have meant rest, where “the wicked cease from troubling, and the weary are at rest” (3:17).
Job says, “For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me” (3:25).
Eliphaz begins gently, asking if Job will be impatient (4:2).
He reminds Job that he has comforted others (4:3-4).
Eliphaz states his principle: “Who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off?” (4:7).
He describes a night vision of a spirit that said, “Can mortal man be in the right before God?” (4:12-17).
interpretation:
Start with Job’s lament. It would be easy to see it as a failure of faith. It is not. Notice who Job is not cursing. In verse 1 he curses the day of his birth, not God. He has not yet said anything against God. That restraint is easy to miss, and the narrator wants you to see that Job is still holding on even as he wishes he were dead.

The lament also shows how deep the grief is. Job does not want to die in order to be rid of God. He wants rest. “There the prisoners are at ease together” (3:18). He is exhausted. There is something very honest in this chapter, and the Bible makes room for it. You do not have to be strong in order to be faithful.

Then comes Eliphaz, and his first speech sounds reasonable. He is kind at first. He is trying to help. But he holds a theory, and the theory is stated in 4:7-8: the innocent do not perish, and “those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same.” If Job is suffering, Job must have sinned. This is the principle of retribution, and it is true in a general way: sin has consequences, and wisdom tends to lead to life. Proverbs says so. But Eliphaz has taken a general truth and turned it into a rule that explains every single case. Job’s suffering does not fit the rule, and so Eliphaz must either change the rule or accuse Job.

The night vision is worth noticing too. Eliphaz claims a spiritual experience as proof. The message he reports, that no human is righteous before God, is true. Paul will say the same in Romans 3. But it is used wrongly here. It is a true statement that Eliphaz uses as a club.

Be careful to read this as a lesson on how to comfort. The friends could have kept silent. They could have wept. Instead they explained. Explaining pain to a person in pain, before you understand it, is not comfort.
connection: Jonah also wished to die (Jonah 4:3), and so did Elijah (1 Kings 19:4), and God cared for both of them. Jesus rejected the same theory of retribution when his disciples asked whether a man’s blindness was caused by his sin or his parents’ (John 9:1-3). “Neither this man nor his parents sinned.”
application:
First, if you have said dark things to God in your pain, take comfort that Job did too, and that Scripture records it without rebuke.

Second, watch yourself when someone else is hurting. Before you offer a reason, offer your presence. Ask yourself whether you are trying to help them or to make yourself feel that the world is safe.

Third, test any belief that says “good people always get good things.” It is not what the Bible says.
prayerPrompts: Bring God your darkest thoughts without hiding them.
Ask him to keep you from explaining away another person’s pain.
Ask him to teach you to sit with those who weep.
